A Motorhome to Ride Out the Apocalypse: This 1980 MAN KAT1 Conversion Wants Your Attention
45 photos
Photo: Car And Classic
No one likes preparing for the worst, there are no finer ways for doing that than with this motorhome, which seems perfect to ride out the apocalypse in. Though it wasn't intentionally designed to withstand whatever the end of times might bring, this 1980 MAN KAT1 motorhome conversion is bound to do just that.
In these troubled times, making a sensible decision is a must. This motorhome won't be that from a financial perspective, but if you're an all doom and gloom type, it would probably feel that way in terms of preparing for the worst.
This overland motorhome isn't just badass enough to handle the collapse of civilization, however it might happen, but it's also a certified historic vehicle, though that last part will mean nothing when the zombies come.
But let's not start this on a negative note. This is a 1980 MAN KAT1 motorhome conversion, with the base vehicle registered as a historic vehicle and coming with the proper documentation and the conversion being a more recent, bespoke job.
Photo: Car And Classic The rig is up for sale on auction through the Car and Classic platform and is now located in Aquitaine, France, where it spent the last four years inside a garage . The current owner bought it in 2022 and oversaw its conversion into a motorhome, and he says that the rig as it is has never been used for overlanding. Photos in the gallery show that it's been appointed for that purpose, even if it never got to fulfill it.
The base of the rig is MAN KAT1, described as "the most renowned military truck platforms for its offroad ability." Even that's an understatement: in production between 1977 and 1983 and offered in 4x4, 6x6, and 8x8 variants, it's the most badass military vehicle produced.
Development for it started as early as 1962, when the West German military announced the intention to replace the aging fleet. Because the list of requirements was so vast and ultimately impossible to check in its entirety, the military asked manufacturers to pool their resources, leading to the foundation of a joint development bureau under MAN.
Photo: Car And Classic During the production years, 10,424 MAN KAT1 units would be built, 3,601 of which would be 4x4s. This was one of them, and the seller is offering full documentation for its military past, including its logbook with personnel transport missions.
For the motorhome conversion, the seller prepped the base vehicle with a full restoration, which included sandblasting and repainting the chassis. The bespoke "living cell" is a four-person home that's fully self-contained – which is to be expected whenever you speak of an overlander but still feels one notch above the rest.
Access inside is done via a solid metal staircase, through a magnet flyscreen, directly into the main living space. Though you can tell from a first glance, it offers sleeping for four people, though it seems only one of the bunks is already prepped for that. The other appears empty and could double as extra storage room.
Photo: Car And Classic So, you get dual enclosed bunks in front of the entryway, a bathroom at the front, a full kitchen on the campside, and a booth dinette that will drop into a bed across the way.
Features are exactly what you'd expect for a "self-contained" RV: a roof lined fully with solar panels, a Victron Energy control unit, a massive battery pack, holding tanks, a Truma Sapphire Compact AC, heater, and the full range of appliances. Unfortunately, the seller doesn't offer exact figures for the solar, battery, or holding tanks.
Everything runs off solar, including kitchen appliances. The large counter integrates a two-burner induction cooktop, a small oven, a compact dishwasher, a mini washing machine (probably a 3 or 4-kg/6.6 or 8.8-lb one), and a 12V fridge. You also get plenty of workspace in here for meal prep and sufficient storage both for kitchen utensils and dry goods.
Photo: Car And Classic The bathroom is a full one as well, with a plumbed toilet, a sink on a vanity, a heated towel rack right above the toilet, and a nice glass-encased shower. It's the most luxurious part of the build, but that doesn't mean that the rest of the space is ugly or cheap in any way. It's rather in keeping with the beefed up exterior, with an emphasis on functionality and space, not necessarily aesthetics.
Also included with the build is a large screen TV, dedicated storage inside the bunks, water filtration, a premium Froli-like system on top of the slatted base of the upper bunk, and plenty of lockable metal lockers outside.
Power for this motorhome comes from the original naturally aspirated 12.8-liter air-cooled Deutz V8 diesel engine located behind the cab and delivering 252 hp and 579 lb ft (785 Nm) of torque. The rig has a 6-speed ZF transmission, permanent four-wheel drive, locking differentials, and hub-reduction gears.
Photo: Car And Classic The seller notes that the paintjob shows some imperfections, as does the three-person cab, particularly on the double seat. The odometer reads 18,484 km (11,485 miles), but as already mentioned, the current owner added nothing to it since they kept the motorhome inside a garage.
The current bid is €8,000 (approximately $8,750 at the current exchange rate) with 6 more days to go into the auction , but reserve hasn't even been met.
